gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aheahe "Zephyr"; Andrews–Parker Ahe n. 3 "a light breeze … Same as aheahe"
verdict_reason: P&E (via POLLEX) lists aheahe "zephyr" under PNP *afe "stir, as a light body in the wind", and Andrews gives ahe "a light breeze … Same as aheahe", so the breeze word is very likely ahe doubled, keeping its sense. Hawaiian Wikipedia song texts use "ka makani aheahe" and "nā aheahe makani". Held because there is no stone to double: AHE needs a glossary line (the protoform *afe is inferred from aheahe's POLLEX set), and P&E must show ahe "breeze" as its own entry. If P&E has no free ahe, drop.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ahiahi ("evening (time of day)"); POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ahiahi "Evening"
verdict_reason: Not fire doubled. Wiktionary derives ahiahi from PPN *afiafi, "a reduplication of Proto-Oceanic *ʀapi" (late afternoon, evening), while ahi "fire" comes from PPN *afi < PAn *Sapuy; POLLEX also keeps *afiafi "evening" apart from *afi "fire". AHI·AHI would print "fire · fire" for evening, a false parts row (DECISIONS C3).

gloss_source: Wiktionary akaaka ("clear, transparent", "luminous, shining")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of aka (bright)", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews has aka v. "to light up, as the moon before rising". "Clear, luminous" is the base sense repeated. Held because the AKA stone joins two etyma: Wiktionary and Andrews put "bright, moon-glow" in one entry with "shadow, reflection" (*qata), but POLLEX gives P&E's aka "moon dawn" its own etymon (PPN *ata). P&E must confirm akaaka "clear" (there is no POLLEX row for it) and which ancestor the stone prints (DECISIONS B8).

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aleale "Wounded, pierced; sound, sore"
verdict_reason: The spelling aleale, without ʻokina, is P&E's "wounded, pierced; sore" (via POLLEX, PPN *aleale, flagged Uncertain Semantic Connection): one morpheme, with no Hawaiian base ale of that meaning. POLLEX's only ale is "hollow or cavern on sea floor", and Andrews' ale is "wave" (= ʻale) and "to swallow". ALE·ALE would be the wrong stones for every reading.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aliali "Crystal clear, white"
verdict_reason: P&E's aliali "crystal clear, white" (via POLLEX) continues PPN *qali "bare, exposed, clearly visible, transparent", which has no free form in Hawaiian in any source in hand (POLLEX lists no Hawaiian ali). Wiktionary treats aniani "glass" as a variant of aliali. The only Hawaiian ali in hand, Andrews' "scar", is not this word's meaning.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aloalo "All kinds of Hibiscus"
verdict_reason: P&E's aloalo (via POLLEX) is the hibiscus, from PSO *kalo-kalo "Erythrina flower" (flagged Problematic): a plant name, not alo "front, face" (PPN *qaro) doubled. Andrews' aloalo builds on a different alo, "dodge". ALO·ALO would print "front · front" for a flower.

gloss_source: Wiktionary aniani ("to be cool, to be refreshing", "to blow softly"); Andrews–Parker Aniani adj., v. ("cool; refreshing … gently blowing")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has a separate aniani "to be cool, refreshing; to blow softly" as a "reduplication of ani" (PPN *aŋi "blow"), and Andrews has aniani "gently blowing, zephyr-like", "a gentle breeze" and "to blow gently, as a wind", matching his ani v. 4 "to blow softly". Held because P&E via POLLEX shows aniani only as "mirror, glass; clear" (*qali) and "travel swiftly" (*aŋi "unencumbered"), so P&E must confirm the breeze sense. The same spelling as a stone (glass, in makaaniani) and as a pair (breeze) also needs the designer's eye (DECISIONS B6).

gloss_source: Wiktionary anuanu ("cold"); Andrews–Parker Anu ("cold; chilliness"), to which Anuanu refers
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of anu", category Hawaiian reduplications, and Andrews sends anuanu to anu. anu "cold" is P&E's via POLLEX (PNP *qanu). The doubled word keeps the base sense, and Hawaiian Wikipedia uses anuanu for cold seasons and climates. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword.

gloss_source: Wiktionary auau ("to walk lightly and swiftly", "to hasten, hurry"); Andrews–Parker Auau v., the second-stressed entry ("to expedite; to hasten; to hurry")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has auau "to walk lightly and swiftly; to hasten" as a "reduplication of au", and Andrews has a separately stressed verb auau "to expedite; to hasten; to hurry". The AU stone is au "current, movement" (PPN *qau), so hurrying shows the base only partly. Andrews' simple "to hurry" sits inside his swim verb, which modern spelling writes ʻau, so P&E must confirm the unglottalized auau "hasten" and that its base is au, not ʻau. Partial transparency also needs a P&E Lit. (DECISIONS C3).

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aʻeaʻe "Banana variety with green and white striped fruit and leaves"
verdict_reason: P&E's aʻeaʻe (via POLLEX) is a banana variety from PMQ *ake "banana variety", not the soapberry / prickly-ash tree aʻe (PPN *ake "Zanthoxylum") doubled. AʻE·AʻE would print "soapberry · soapberry" for a banana.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) aʻiaʻi "Bright as moonlight; fair, white, clear, pure, brilliant, shining"
verdict_reason: P&E's aʻiaʻi "bright as moonlight; clear, white" (via POLLEX) continues PCE *akiaki, reconstructed already doubled. No source in hand has a Hawaiian aʻi "bright", so there is no base to double.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) epaepa "Part of a fish's tail above and below the cleft"
verdict_reason: Two different words share the spelling. Andrews' epaepa ("See epa") is epa "deceitful" doubled, but epa has no Wiktionary entry, so there is no stone, and the sense is a put-down. P&E's epaepa (via POLLEX) is the part of a fish's tail above and below the cleft, filed under PPN *qepa "ceremonial mats" with an uncertain link, and is not epa doubled.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) haha "Net gauge"
verdict_reason: P&E's two haha (via POLLEX) are single morphemes: "net gauge" (PPN *qafa) and "proud, haughty" (PPN *fasa, uncertain). There is no short-vowel ha stone: Wiktionary's roots are hā "four", "breath" and "leaf stalk", all with kahakō, so HA·HA would be the wrong stones and a different spelling (§4.4).

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) hakahaka "Vacant space, vacancy, room; blanks, gap"; Wiktionary hakahaka ("vacancy", "gap", "blank space")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of haka (breach)", category Hawaiian reduplications; POLLEX puts P&E's hakahaka "vacant space, gap" in the same set as P&E's haka "hole, breach, open space, vacancy" (PNP *fata "gape; gap"), and Andrews' hakahaka ends "See haka, n." All sources name haka#1, and the doubled word plainly keeps its sense. Spelling attested. Living use on Hawaiian Wikipedia ("Ua 1,000 mau makahiki kēia hakahaka").

gloss_source: Wiktionary hakuhaku ("lumpy"); Andrews–Parker Hakuhaku adj. ("Full of hard lumps; lumpy")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of haku (lump)", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews has hakuhaku adj. "full of hard lumps; lumpy" beside haku n. 2 "a hard lump of anything". Both name the lump sense (haku#1; POLLEX P&E haku "stone", PPN *fatu), and "lumpy" is that sense repeated. Spelling attested in Wiktionary and POLLEX. POLLEX shows P&E's hakuhaku only as "fold", so the P&E check should confirm "lumpy".

gloss_source: Wiktionary halahala ("correction", "criticism, reproach", "complaint")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hala (to sin, to err)", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews: "[Redup. of hala, to miss.] See hala." Both name hala#0 (PPN *sala "err, error"), and finding fault is the base sense repeated. Spelling attested. P&E should confirm the criticism sense, since POLLEX lists only the fish homograph.

gloss_source: Wiktionary halehale ("towering", "cavernous"); Andrews–Parker Halehale adj. ("deep, as a cavern")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary calls halehale a reduplication of hale "house" (compare Māori wharewhare "overhanging"), but its meanings (towering, cavernous, deep as a pit) do not plainly show "house", and Andrews gives no bracket. HALE·HALE would print "house · house" for "cavernous" and link it to the 19 hale words. It could stand only with a P&E Lit. reading tying it to house (DECISIONS C3).

gloss_source: Wiktionary hanahana ("hot, warm", "vehement"); Andrews–Parker Hanahana adj. 1 ("Warm, as a hot day; heated, as with exercise")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hana (warm)", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews' hanahana "warm, as a hot day" refers to "the root, hana", and the warmth is the base sense intensified. Held because Andrews says the verb is "more properly written hahana", and modern use also has hanahana "work". P&E must say which spelling it gives for "warm" and whether its hanahana is "warm" or "work". The hana#1 stone also needs a glossary line (the glossary batches so far define hana#0 only).

gloss_source: Wiktionary hanohano ("distinguished, honored, dignified"; "distinction, honor"); Andrews–Parker Hanohano adj., n. ("Glorious; honored; dignified")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hano (glorious)", category Hawaiian reduplications, and Andrews' hanohano "glorious; honored; dignified" carries the same sense, so the doubled word keeps it as an intensive. Spelling attested. Held only because the free base hano "glorious" rests on Wiktionary alone: P&E must show it as its own entry, or the HANO stone has nothing under it.

gloss_source: Wiktionary hauhau ("cold (as food)"); Andrews–Parker Hauhau adj. ("Cold; applied to food that has become cold")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: hauhau "cold (as food)", "Reduplication of hau", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews agrees on "cold, applied to food". But POLLEX files P&E's hauhau "bad odour; cool" as one word under PPN *fau-fau "disgusting" (Māori houhou "cold, disagreeable"), not under hau "dew, cool" (*sau). The sources split on the base, so P&E must show whether the "cool" hauhau is listed with hau.

gloss_source: Wiktionary haʻahaʻa ("lowly, low", "humble, meek", "modest, unassuming"); Andrews–Parker Haahaa v. ("to be low; humble")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of haʻa (low)", category Hawaiian reduplications; Andrews–Parker writes ha'a-ha'a, "to be low; humble". Low becomes lowly, humble, so the doubled word keeps the base sense. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword, and Hawaiian Wikipedia uses it about 39 times (noi haʻahaʻa, kula haʻahaʻa). Neither the word nor haʻa "low" has a §4.3 sense. P&E should confirm the low/humble senses: POLLEX has haʻa only as "dwarf, short in stature".

gloss: a place in Puna, east Hawaiʻi
gloss_source: POLLEX haʻehaʻe "(place near easternmost point of Hawaiʻi)", from Pukui, Elbert & Mookini 1974
exclusion_reasons: mainly a proper name: the only spelled source (POLLEX, from Pukui, Elbert & Mookini's place names) gives haʻehaʻe as a place in Puna; Andrews also lists it as a cape in Puna and as the enclosures before a temple of Lono
verdict_reason: There is no base haʻe: no Wiktionary or POLLEX entry and no stone id. The one source for the ʻokina spelling is a place name (POLLEX, *sa-sake "east", flagged Problematic). The tearing word Andrews gives is hae/haehae, a different spelling, and its senses include a beast rending a person. As HAʻE·HAʻE it would be mainly a proper name with no root behind it.

gloss_source: Wiktionary haʻihaʻi ("brittle", "quavering, breaking"; reduplication of haʻi "to break"); Andrews–Parker Haihai adj. ("brittle; easily broken") and v. [Hai, to break] ("to break in pieces")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary analyses haʻihaʻi as a reduplication of haʻi "to break" (brittle, breaking), and Andrews brackets it [Freq. of hai] / [Hai, to break]: a frequentative that keeps the base sense. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword. Not a keep because haʻi sits under the A17 P&E gate (Andrews' lascivious sense under hai/hoohai, echoed in haihai v. 6). If P&E has no such sense on haʻi "break", this becomes a keep.

gloss_source: Wiktionary heahea ("frequentative of hea (call)", "to welcome", "friendly, hospitable"); Andrews–Parker Heahea v. [Redup. of hea] ("to call frequently … to call in; to welcome")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hea (to call)", category Hawaiian reduplications, glossed as the frequentative of hea; Andrews brackets [Redup. of hea]: call, call often, call in, welcome. The base sense plainly carries through. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword and matches Andrews. No §4.3 sense on heahea or on hea#0. P&E should confirm (no POLLEX row for heahea).

gloss_source: Wiktionary heihei ("race (test of speed)", "to race"); Andrews–Parker Heihei v. ("to run a race")
verdict_reason: No source analyses heihei as hei doubled. Wiktionary gives no etymology, Andrews gives no bracket, and hei has no Wiktionary entry (no stone id). Its senses (net, snare, cat's cradle; POLLEX hei "cat's cradle", PNP *fai) have nothing to do with racing. heihei is a lexical reduplication with no free base, so HEI·HEI would print a false parts row.

gloss_source: POLLEX hekeheke "plump" (P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hekeheke adj. ("very fleshy")
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts hekeheke "plump" under PPN *fete "swollen" and heke "shy, sensitive" under PCE *fete "cautious, timid": two separate sets, so plump is not shy doubled. Andrews' heke ("chagrined; sensitive"; "a peg; a sail") has no swelling sense either, and heke has no Wiktionary entry or stone id. The word does not keep a sense of any attested base.

gloss_source: Wiktionary helahela verb ("to spread one's arms", reduplication of hela "to spread the arms"); POLLEX hela "spread (arms)" (P&E 1986)
verdict_reason: Wiktionary analyses both senses of helahela as reduplications of hela (category Hawaiian reduplications), and the "spread the arms" sense matches P&E's hela via POLLEX. But hela has no Wiktionary entry, so there is no stone id, and the sources name two different hela (redness; spread arms) behind one doubled word. The sense cannot be pinned to one stone from these sources. Admit only if P&E gives helahela "spread the arms" as a reduplication of hela "spread" and a HELA stone is curated.

gloss_source: Wiktionary heluhelu ("to read", "to count"); Andrews–Parker Heluhelu v. ("to read; to pore over; to recount")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of helu", category Hawaiian reduplications, with both "to read" and "to count". Andrews: to read; to recount. Reading builds on counting (going over item by item) without saying so, so the link is partial (per the brief). Spelling is a Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense. Held at keep-pending because a partial word needs P&E's reading of it (C3); P&E should confirm the "count" sense on heluhelu.

gloss_source: Wiktionary hemahema ("awkward, clumsy", "unskilled"; reduplication of hema "left"); Andrews–Parker Hemahema adv., v. ("incompetently"; "to be inefficient")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hema (left)", category Hawaiian reduplications. The doubled word means awkward, clumsy: left-like, a figurative likeness the reader has to supply, so the link is partial. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword, matching Andrews. No §4.3 sense on the word or on hema. Held at keep-pending because a partial word needs P&E's reading (C3).

gloss_source: Wiktionary henehene ("to mock, tease, laugh at"; reduplication of hene "to snicker"); Andrews–Parker Henehene v. ("to laugh in derision; to mock")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of hene (to snicker)", category Hawaiian reduplications, and hene lists henehene "mock" among its derived terms. Snicker becomes laugh at, tease: an intensive that keeps the base sense. Spelling is a Wiktionary headword, matching Andrews. No §4.3 sense. P&E check is routine (no POLLEX row).

gloss_source: POLLEX heʻaheʻa ("to imprint with spots, stains; smeared, as with red earth", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Heahea v. [Redupl. of hea, to redden]
exclusion_reasons: base heʻa: P&E via POLLEX glosses it "stained red; destroyed; blood sacrifice" (etymon *feka-feka "entrails"), and Andrews' red/bloody hea entry describes choosing a human sacrifice at a heiau. This is a temple death rite, the class §4.3 keeps out with sorcery and death-prayer
verdict_reason: The repeat is likely: Andrews brackets [Redupl. of hea, to redden], and POLLEX files heʻa and heʻaheʻa under the same *feka-feka, so stained red becomes smeared with red. But heʻa has no Wiktionary entry (no stone id), and its P&E sense includes "blood sacrifice", with Andrews describing the selection of a human sacrifice. It is excluded under §4.3 on the base.

gloss_source: Wiktionary heʻe (verb) derived terms: heʻeheʻe "avalanche" (a derived-term list, not a headword)
verdict_reason: heʻeheʻe as heʻe "slide" doubled (avalanche, landslide) appears only in Wiktionary's list of heʻe's derived terms, with no headword, sense or source. The spelled dictionary entry (P&E via POLLEX) is an unrelated breast disease, and Andrews rejects the form for heheʻe. If P&E lists heʻeheʻe "to slide; landslide" under heʻe, this becomes keep-pending on heʻe#1 (still under the A16 gate).

gloss_source: Wiktionary hihi ("to entangle, to intertwine", "to creep, to spread"); POLLEX hihi ("entangle, creep, spread, intertwine", P&E 1986)
exclusion_reasons: base hi/hī: P&E via POLLEX hī "dysentery, diarrhoea" (PNP *sii) and Andrews hi "a flowing away; a purging; dysentery", "to purge": excretory
verdict_reason: hihi is one morpheme, PNP *fifi "entangled" (Wiktionary and POLLEX), not hi doubled. There is no base hi with an entangling sense, and no stone id. The only base senses in hand are hī "fish with a line" and hī "dysentery" (P&E via POLLEX), and Andrews' purging sense, which also exclude it.

gloss_source: POLLEX hilahila ("bashful, shameful, ashamed", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hilahila adj., n., v. ("ashamed"; "shame")
verdict_reason: POLLEX derives hilahila from CC *sila "shy, bashful", and the doubled form is the Hawaiian word. No source gives a free hila "shy": Andrews' only hila is "same as ohila", Wiktionary has none, and there is no stone id. HILA·HILA would print a root that does not exist on its own.

gloss_source: Wiktionary hinahina ("Heliotropium anomalum, a heliotrope of the Pacific Islands"); POLLEX hinahina ("various plant spp. (Heliotropium anomalum)", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hinahina adj. ("grayish; gray")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: from PPN *sinasina, "by surface analysis, reduplication of hina", in Hawaiian reduplications, and hina "gray hair" lists hinahina as related. Andrews gives hinahina "grayish; gray", which plainly keeps the base. But the dictionary headword sense (Wiktionary; P&E via POLLEX, PCE *sina-sina "a plant") is a plant whose link to gray the sources leave implicit, so the link is partial. Spelling is attested in both. No §4.3 sense. P&E should confirm the gray sense or a Lit. reading.

gloss_source: POLLEX hinihini ("faint, as voice", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hinihini n. ("speaking in a small, thin voice; whispering") and Hini hini adj. ("indistinct; faint (applied to the voice)")
verdict_reason: POLLEX files hinihini under an unreduplicated PCE *hini "faint (of voice)", and Andrews has a free hini "small; thin; feeble". Thin and feeble becomes a faint voice, so the base sense carries through. But hini rests on Andrews alone: no Wiktionary entry, no POLLEX row for the Hawaiian base, and no stone id. A card would print an Andrews-only root gloss (F1). It becomes keep-pending if P&E lists hini "thin, faint" and a HINI stone is curated.

gloss_source: POLLEX hinuhinu ("bright, glossy, shining, lustrous … splendid", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hinuhinu v. ("to be bright; glistening; shining"); Hinu hinu adj. ("glittering, as polished stones")
verdict_reason: POLLEX gives P&E's hinuhinu under PPN *sinu-sinu "oily, shiny", the reduplication of hinu's *sinu, and Wiktionary lists hinuhinu as hinu's reduplicated form. Polished and lustrous become bright, glossy: an intensive that keeps the base sense. The spelling is P&E's via POLLEX, matching Andrews. No §4.3 sense on the word or the base.

gloss_source: POLLEX hiohio ("whistle softly; blow softly", P&E 1986); Wiktionary hio derived terms (hiohio "whistle softly")
exclusion_reasons: base hio: Wiktionary gives "to fart silently" under the same etymology as "to blow in gusts" (PNP *fio), and Andrews hio n. 3 is "a passage of wind from the bowels". This is excretory, and A17 places the sense on hio (short vowels)
verdict_reason: It is a real repeat: Wiktionary lists hiohio under hio, POLLEX puts both under PNP *fio "whistle", and blow in gusts becomes blow or whistle softly. But the HIO stone carries an excretory sense in Wiktionary (same etymology) and in Andrews. §4.3 removes the word when any sense of the base is excretory and a reader may know it.

gloss_source: POLLEX hiwahiwa ("precious, beloved, esteemed", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hiwahiwa adj. ("precious; esteemed; greatly beloved")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary lists hiwahiwa among hiwa's derived terms, but POLLEX files P&E's hiwahiwa under a different PPN *siwa, "dance and sing" (flagged Problematic), not hiwa "black" (PCE *siwa). Either way "precious, beloved" does not keep "entirely black", so HIWA·HIWA would read black + black = beloved. The sense is unresolved and the word opaque (C3).

gloss_source: POLLEX hiʻohiʻo ("ruddy, bright red", P&E 1986); Andrews–Parker Hiohio adj. ("ruddy; bright red: ula hiohio")
verdict_reason: There is no base hiʻo: no Wiktionary entry, no POLLEX row and no stone id. POLLEX ties hiʻohiʻo to PCE *hiko "twinkle, flash, shine" only with "Uncertain Semantic Connection". The doubled word is a colour term with no free root behind it, so HIʻO·HIʻO would print an empty part.

gloss_source: Wiktionary melemele ("light yellow (color)"); Andrews–Parker Mele adj. 2 ("Yellow; generally written melemele")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary analyses melemele as a reduplication of mele "to be yellow" (category Hawaiian reduplications), and Andrews says mele "yellow" is "generally written melemele": the doubled word keeps the base sense. Headword spelling attested in Wiktionary. No §4.3 sense on the word or on mele#1. P&E should confirm the colour sense of melemele (only the star-name homograph is in POLLEX).

gloss_source: Wiktionary mikomiko ("lightly salted", "delicious"); Andrews–Parker Mikomiko adj. ("relishable, as food; seasoned")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of miko (seasoned)" (Hawaiian reduplications); Andrews brackets [Miko, to be salty]. Seasoned/salted → lightly salted, tasty keeps the base sense. Wiktionary headword spelling. No POLLEX row; P&E check is routine.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): milimili "to examine with interest or curiosity and admiration"; Andrews–Parker Milimili n. 2 ("a favorite … especially cherished")
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts mili "handle" and milimili in one P&E-sourced set (PPN *mili), and Andrews brackets milimili [Mili, to handle]: a reduplication of this base. The meaning moves from handling to admiring and cherishing, so the sense is partly kept. No Wiktionary entry exists for mili, so there is no stone id yet: "mili" is proposed as a new stone (gloss "handle", *mili). Pending P&E for the stone and the gloss.

exclusion_reasons: excretory: the word's main sense (Wiktionary, Andrews)
verdict_reason: Excretory (§4.3). Not a doubling either: Wiktionary derives mimi whole from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *mimi, and Andrews' mi is a short form of mimi, not its base.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): moamoa "sharp point at the stern of a canoe"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary and Andrews' bracket call moamoa a reduplication of moa "fowl", but no usable sense keeps "fowl". "To care for, supply with food" is Andrews' synonym of momoa ("to give liberally"), and the P&E word (canoe stern point) comes from a separate etymon, PNP *moa "notched ornamentation at end of canoe", which is not a moa stone. MOA·MOA would link falsely to the chicken words (huamoa, hakamoa).

gloss_source: Wiktionary muʻumuʻu ("to be cut off, shortened")
verdict_reason: No source analyses muʻumuʻu as muʻu doubled. Wiktionary has no muʻu, and Andrews' only muʻu ("collected, laid up in store") is unrelated to "cut short". Its other senses (amputee; the dress) would not make good cards anyway.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): māmā "light (in weight)"; Wiktionary māmā ("nimble, quick")
verdict_reason: The reduplication happened long before Hawaiian: PPN *maqa-maqa "light in weight", which Wiktionary traces to Proto-Oceanic *maʀaqan. The only Hawaiian base mā means "clear, faded" (PPN *maqa "clean, light-coloured"), a different etymon, so MĀ·MĀ would teach a false split. māmā is a good word as a single stone (DECISIONS B7b).

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Mumu v. ("to be silent; to be mum"), Mumu v. ("to hum; to mumble"); POLLEX (P&E) mū "silent; to shut the lips and make no sound"
verdict_reason: Andrews gives mū v. "to shut the lips … same as mumu; to be silent" and mumu v. "to be silent; to be mum", with "to hum; to mumble". POLLEX's PNP *muu "be silent" set has reduplicated cognates for murmuring (Tahitian mû/mû, Rapa Nui mu/muu "taciturn"). So MŪ·MŪ keeps mū#4. But the only attested mūmū (P&E via POLLEX) means "blunt", so the spelling for the silent/hum sense is inferred. P&E must confirm that mūmū carries this sense and is spelled with both kahakō.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): nahenahe "soft, gentle, suave"; Wiktionary nahenahe ("soft", "sweet, melodious")
verdict_reason: Andrews has nahe "soft, gentle, as the voice of music; to blow softly", says nahenahe is "same as nahe", and uses nahe "gently" in kolonahe. The doubled word keeps the base sense. But Wiktionary and POLLEX derive nahenahe whole from PPN *gase-gase, and nahe is in neither, so there is no stone id: "nahe" is proposed as a new stone. Pending P&E for the base nahe.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nana ("Lānaʻi form of ulana")
exclusion_reasons: base is grammatical: na/nā is a possessive particle and the plural article (POLLEX *na; Andrews)
verdict_reason: Not a doubling of na. nana is a Lānaʻi dialect form of ulana, and the base is a particle. Andrews' "to gaze at" is nānā, written without its kahakō.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nananana ("spider"); Andrews–Parker Nananana n. 1
verdict_reason: Andrews gives nananana as "same as lanalana" (spider; outrigger lashing; to float, from lana "float"). No source derives it from nana, the Lānaʻi form of ulana "to plait". A link between spider and plaiting would be our own guess.

gloss_source: Wiktionary naonao ("ant"); POLLEX (P&E) naonao "ants"
exclusion_reasons: Andrews homograph naonao "phlegm; spittle; mucus from the nose" (bodily discharge; Andrews-only, so a P&E gate under DECISIONS A1)
verdict_reason: The reduplicated form is inherited whole: PPN *nao-nao "sandfly, midge". Hawaiian nao is "ripple, groove" (*gao) or "probe" (*nao), so neither matches. Not NAO·NAO.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Naunau v. [Nau, to bite] ("to chew; to mince in the mouth"); POLLEX (P&E) nau "chew"
verdict_reason: Andrews brackets the verb naunau [Nau, to bite], "to chew; to move the jaws as in eating", a frequentative of nau "chew" (P&E via POLLEX, PPN *gau). The sense is kept. But the verb sense is Andrews-only: the attested naunau in P&E is the plant. No Wiktionary entry for nau, so "nau" (chew, *gau) is proposed as a new stone, to be split from the other nau homographs. P&E must confirm a naunau "chew" entry.

gloss_source: Wiktionary naʻanaʻa ("protruding")
exclusion_reasons: Andrews sense "a state of costiveness" (constipation): excretory
verdict_reason: No source attests a base naʻa. Wiktionary's derivation from naʻa "firmly seated" is marked "perhaps", and "potbellied" and "sour-tempered" do not build on it. It also has an excretory Andrews sense.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): nene "fretting, teasing or nagging for something"
verdict_reason: Andrews' ne ("to be teased; to be fretful; to droop") fits nene "fretting, teasing" (P&E), so it is likely a repeat. But: POLLEX derives nene whole from PNP *gege "weary"; the base ne is Andrews-only and has no stone; the gloss teaches little and borders on a put-down; the spelling invites misreading as nēnē; and the same spelling carries a sexual etymon. Together these are enough to leave it out.

gloss: plump and full, as ripe fruit
gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Newe (newenewe adj. 1: "plump; full … as a round, full grown fruit"); POLLEX (P&E) newenewe "plump"
verdict_reason: Andrews brackets newenewe [Newe, to be large], and newe "large, round and full" carries into "plump, full", so the sense is kept. But the base newe is Andrews-only, with no Wiktionary or POLLEX entry and no stone. POLLEX reconstructs the doubled form whole (PMQ *newenewe). The P&E-attested sense is about a pregnant body, so a fruit gloss would rest on Andrews alone. Needs P&E for newe and the kumu's ear before it can be kept.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nihoniho ("to be toothed, notched, serrated"); Andrews–Parker Nihoniho adj. ("set with teeth, as a saw")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: "Reduplication of niho (tooth)" (Hawaiian reduplications), with the Malay gigi/gerigi parallel; Andrews "set with teeth, as a saw". Tooth → toothed, serrated is a plain likeness reduplication. The spelling is a Wiktionary headword, and the base niho is PPN *nifo (POLLEX, P&E). Nothing to exclude.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nini ("to pour", "balm, ointment"); POLLEX (P&E) nini "pour, spill", "ointment, balm"
verdict_reason: No Hawaiian base ni exists in any source. nini is inherited whole (CC *nigi "pour out"; PPN *nini "smear"), and Andrews calls it the root form of ninini. It could be a single stone, but it is not NI·NI.

gloss: many; a small gnat or ant
gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): lonalona, nonanona "many"; Andrews–Parker Nonanona n. 1 ("a small gnat; also a species of ant")
exclusion_reasons: base is grammatical: nona is a possessive pronoun "his, hers, its" (Andrews)
verdict_reason: Not nona doubled. P&E (via POLLEX) gives nonanona as a variant of lonalona "many" (PPN *loga), and Andrews as "a small gnat; ant". The base nona is a possessive pronoun.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): nono "oozing, seeping out (as water in the sand)"; Wiktionary nono ("oozing, seeping")
verdict_reason: Andrews has no "to leak, as water under ground from a taro patch; to ooze out" and no "seepage", which fits nono "oozing, seeping" (P&E). But POLLEX derives nono whole from PPN *gogo "suck liquid"; the base no "seep" is Andrews-only with no stone (Wiktionary and POLLEX have only the particle no); and the word's other senses (red-faced; holey) do not keep it. Keep-pending only if P&E lists no "seep" as a word of its own.

gloss_source: Wiktionary noʻonoʻo (verb 'to think, reflect'; noun 'thought, reflection')
verdict_reason: A doubled noʻo only on Andrews' word: Noonoo is bracketed [Noo, to think], and Noo is 'primitive form of noonoo … used only in noonoo'. Wiktionary gives no etymology. noʻo has no Wiktionary entry and no POLLEX row, so there is no stone id. Sense is left unresolved until a NOʻO stone ('reflect, turn over in the mind') is curated; the proposed id is 'noʻo'. Until then the stone links to nothing. P&E needs to confirm noʻo as a root.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) nunu 'Swollen, puffed up; to swell'
verdict_reason: Not nu doubled. In Wiktionary, nunu is the Lānaʻi form of lunu 'greed'. POLLEX gives 'swollen, to swell' (< PPN *gugu, itself a reduplicated etymon) and 'swathe, roll up' (< PMQ *gugu). The short base nu has no Wiktionary or POLLEX entry. Andrews' 'groaning, cooing' sense belongs with nū / nūnū, since Andrews writes no long vowels.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nānā verb 'to look, observe'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Look at, see, observe'
verdict_reason: nānā 'look' comes from PCE *naa-naa 'look at', which was already reduplicated in the proto-language (Wiktionary, POLLEX NAA-NAA). No Hawaiian nā means 'look'. The only lexical nā stone is 'calm, pacified' (< *naqa); the other nā rows are 'moan' (*gaa), the plural article and a demonstrative particle. Doubling the stone would draw a false line to nā 'calm'. nānā already serves as one stone (nānā#1) in the word list.

gloss_source: Wiktionary nēnē verb 'to chirp, to croak', noun 'whimpering'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Chirp … croak … cry, whimper'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives the chirp/whimper verb from a reduplication of *ŋee 'squealing sound', and POLLEX puts nēnē under PEP *gee. The base nē, though, has no Wiktionary entry or POLLEX row; only Andrews' ne 'to murmur, fretful' supports it. So there is no stone id, and the stone would link to nothing. The word's living sense, the goose, is a separate imitative homograph, so it cannot lead under a NĒ·NĒ split (F1).

gloss_source: Wiktionary nūnū 'pigeon'; Andrews–Parker 1922 Nunu n. 2 'A dove; a pigeon'
verdict_reason: Plausibly the bird named for its sound. Andrews gives nu n. 3 'the cooing of doves', and nunu adj. 'cooing like doves' and n. 'a dove; a pigeon'. The nū stone ('grunt; to cough, roar', < PPN *guu 'hum, groan, grunt') is the only homograph, so the sense id is clear. Wiktionary gives no etymology and POLLEX has no nūnū row, so the derivation needs P&E. Sense is kept only partly: it names the bird by its call.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker 1922 Oeoe adj. 'Long; applied to the neck'
verdict_reason: The only Pukui & Elbert oeoe in POLLEX is the storm petrel, from PCE *oi 'petrel', not from oe. A doubled oe ('prolonged sound or thing', P&E via POLLEX OE) is supported only by Andrews, who has oeoe 'long (of a neck)' and uses oeoe for 'whizzing' under Oe. Neither word nor base is in Wiktionary, so there is no stone id, and the gloss rests on Andrews alone.

gloss: tall and straight, as a tree
gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) oheohe 'Tall and straight (as a tree)'
verdict_reason: POLLEX derives oheohe from PCE *kofe-kofe, the bamboo etymon doubled, whose plain Hawaiian reflex is ʻohe (written with ʻokina in POLLEX and Wiktionary). POLLEX's P&E form 'Oheohe' has no ʻokina, though, and the candidate base 'ohe' is not a stone (ʻOHE and OHE are different stones, §4.4). Before the word can be ʻOHE·ʻOHE, P&E must settle whether it is ʻoheʻohe. Even then, 'tall and straight' keeps the bamboo sense only by likeness.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) oioi 'Squirm, leisurely swaying'
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts oioi under PNP *oqi 'shake, agitate, move around'. It puts the base oi 'move, pull away as in anger' under a different etymon, PPN *oi 'withdraw' (OI.1). So oioi doubles another oi, not this one. Neither word nor base is in Wiktionary (only ʻoi 'sharp', a different stone), so there is no stone to link.

gloss_source: Wiktionary okaoka 'bits, particles'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'Dust; small particles; dregs'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives okaoka from PPN *qota-qota, the doubled form of oka's etymon *qota 'dregs' (Wiktionary oka, POLLEX QOTA.2). Andrews brackets it '[Intensive of oka, refuse]'. oka has a single homograph, so the sense id is clear. 'Bits, particles' from 'dregs, crumbs' is a plain intensive or plural.

gloss_source: Wiktionary paepae noun 'platform; pavement; prop, support'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'a pavement of stones; a platform'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives paepae from PPN *pae-pae 'stone surround of a structure', the doubled form of pae#1's etymon PPN *pae 'heap of stones' (pae#1: 'row; cluster; bank; stage, level; platform'; POLLEX PAE.1B 'Cluster, row, bank'). Andrews' Pae v. 2 'to lift, to raise a little. See paepae' agrees. pae#0 'come ashore' (< *paqe) is a separate stone and is not used.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker 1922 Pakapaka v. [Paka, to drop] 'To drop, as large rain drops … to patter'; n. 1 'A heavy shower of rain'
verdict_reason: The patter-of-rain sense is paka#4 doubled ('the sound of raindrops falling', onomatopoeic; P&E via POLLEX paka 'raindrops, patter of rain, esp. big drops'). Andrews brackets it [Paka, to drop]. That sense of pakapaka is Andrews-only, however. POLLEX's only P&E pakapaka is 'wrinkled, scaly' under a different *pata set ('blemish on skin'). P&E must confirm that pakapaka carries the rain sense before the gloss can ship (F1).

gloss_source: Wiktionary palapala 'print or document … writing of any kind'
exclusion_reasons: base PALA carries an excretory sense in the same etymon: P&E via POLLEX pala 'dab of excreta' (PALA.1C, PNP *pala 'mud, dirt, filth, excrement'), which is also the etymon Wiktionary gives for pala 'to smear, daub'; base PALA carries a disease sense, 'form of syphilis' (P&E via POLLEX PALA.3; Andrews 'the syphilis')
verdict_reason: It is a true repeat: Wiktionary says 'Reduplication of pala (to dab, to blot)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and Andrews has [Pala, to paint; to spot]. But a two-stone PALA·PALA would put the PALA stone on the board, and §4.3 and A12 exclude it. Drop it as a repeat. palapala stays a single stone, as the word list already uses it.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) palupalu 'Weak, soft, limber, flexible …'
verdict_reason: POLLEX derives palupalu from PCE *paru 'soft, weak'. No Hawaiian palu with that sense is in the sources. The palu stone is Wiktionary's 'to lick'; P&E's palu rows are 'thresh, beat' (*palu 'knead') and 'fish-head bait' (*paru 'ground-bait'), each a separate set. palupalu keeps none of these senses.

gloss_source: Wiktionary panepane 'to talk back'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of pane (to answer)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. Andrews brackets [Pane, to speak]. pane has one Wiktionary homograph ('answer; to answer, reply'). 'Answer back' is a plain frequentative/intensive. P&E's pane 'hind part of the head; summit' (POLLEX PANE.A) is a separate root and is not used.

gloss_source: Wiktionary papa 'board, lumber; flat surface, layer'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Board'; 'Flat hard surface'
verdict_reason: papa 'board, flat surface' is one inherited morpheme: PPN *papa < Proto-Oceanic *papan < PMP *papan (Wiktionary; POLLEX PAPA.1A–1C). It is not pa doubled. The short base pa has no Wiktionary entry. Andrews' 'reduplication of the distributive particle pa' is the grammatical papa- (papa lua 'twofold'), and it cannot be a stone. PAPA already works as one stone (papa#0, papa#1) in the word list.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) paʻipaʻi 'Trim, prune, cut, clip, as a plant or the hair'
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts paʻipaʻi 'trim, prune' under PPN *paki 'pick, cut off, break off (fruit, leaves)'. The paʻi stone ('hit, slap, clap; print', Wiktionary; POLLEX *paki 'slap, clap; hit') is a different *paki set. So the doubled word keeps no sense of this stone. The word would reopen only if P&E gives paʻipaʻi a 'clap or slap repeatedly' sense, which no source here shows.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pekapeka verb 'to tattle', noun 'tattler'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of peka (tattle)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. Andrews agrees: peka 'to speak of another in a fault-finding manner'. But peka has no Wiktionary entry and no POLLEX row, so there is no stone id. Sense stays unresolved until a PEKA stone is curated (proposed id 'peka'), and the base needs P&E.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pekupeku 'frequentative of peku'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'To kick frequently'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of peku (to kick)', a frequentative, in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. Andrews has [Freq. of peku] 'to kick frequently'. peku has one homograph ('to kick; kick' < PCP *petu; POLLEX PETU 'Kick; ward off'), so the sense id is clear.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pelapela 'filthy, dirty … unclean'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Filthy, dirty, nasty … unclean'
exclusion_reasons: the doubled word's own senses include 'indecent, vulgar, lewd, obscene' (Wiktionary; P&E via POLLEX 'indecent'); the doubled word's senses include 'filth, refuse; to stink' (Wiktionary, Andrews)
verdict_reason: POLLEX gives pelapela < PPN *pela 'mud, dirt, filth', and Andrews brackets [Pela, unclean]. The base's only P&E row, pela 'decayed flesh' (*pera), is a different etymon, and pela has no Wiktionary entry. Whatever the derivation, §4.3 excludes the word on its own senses.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) peʻapeʻa 'Entangled (fig.), perplexity'
exclusion_reasons: base stone peʻa#1 ('cross; to cross') includes 'to menstruate' in Wiktionary, under the same homograph; Andrews pea adj. 'filthy; unclean; … belonging to menstruation'
verdict_reason: Andrews' peapea 'to weave cross-wise … as in lattice work' and 'twisted; braided or woven together' build on peʻa 'cross' (peʻa#1; POLLEX PEP *peka 'a cross, crosswise'). POLLEX, however, puts P&E's peʻapeʻa 'entangled, perplexity' under a separate set, PCE *peka-peka 'trouble, perplexed'. Either way the word would sit on the PEʻA#1 stone, which carries a menstrual sense. §4.3 excludes it.

gloss_source: Wiktionary piapia noun sense 1; Andrews–Parker 1922 Piapia n. 1
exclusion_reasons: genital: P&E via POLLEX glosses piapia 'discharge from eyes' together with a genital secretion; slur: Wiktionary sense 2 is an abusive epithet for an unwashed person, said to refer to the genitals
verdict_reason: §4.3 excludes it on its own senses. It is not pia doubled either: Wiktionary and POLLEX derive it from PPN *pia 'sticky secretion', a separate etymon from pia#0 'arrowroot, starch' (PPN *pia 'arrowroot'). pia#1 'beer' is an English loan, and pia#2 'stork' has no etymology.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pikipiki verb 'to pinch, to squeeze'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'To pinch; to squeeze, as in milking'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of piki (shrunk)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. But piki has no Wiktionary entry and no POLLEX row, so there is no stone id; only Andrews gives piki 'to cut short; to shorten'. Pinching is a short step from 'shrunk, cut short', not a plain intensive, so the sense is kept only partly. Proposed stone id 'piki'. P&E must confirm piki as a free root and its sense.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker 1922 Pilipili adj. [Pili, to adhere] 'Adhering, sticking to; connected with'
verdict_reason: Andrews brackets the adjective [Pili, to adhere], and Hawaiian Wikipedia uses pilipili for closeness (ka pilipili ʻana me nā mea hoʻolohe). But the only P&E row (via POLLEX) is pilipili 'an herb', from PCE *piri-piri 'burr', an inherited plant name rather than a Hawaiian doubling. The spelling is attested. The 'adhering, close' sense rests on Andrews and usage, so P&E must confirm it before the gloss ships (F1).

gloss_source: Wiktionary piopio noun 'chick; sound used to call chickens'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of pio (peep)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. pio#2 is 'peep; to chirp', so the sense id is clear: the chick is named for its peeping. On the language evidence it is a keep. It is held only for the ʻanāʻanā sense Andrews records under piopio. If P&E puts that sense only under hoʻopiopio, it becomes keep.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pipi noun 'Pinctada radiata, Hawaiian pearl oyster'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Shellfish sp.'
verdict_reason: Not pi doubled. The oyster is PPN *pipi 'a bivalve shellfish', one inherited morpheme (POLLEX), and 'cattle, beef' is borrowed from English. Only Andrews pairs pi 'slow to burn' with pipi 'smouldering', and lists pipi as a synonym of pi 'to sprinkle'. Andrews writes no long vowels, so whether that word is pipi or pīpī is unknown, and pi has no Wiktionary entry or POLLEX row to give it a stone.

gloss_source: Wiktionary piʻipiʻi verb 'to bubble forth, to effervesce; effervescent, sparkling'; Andrews–Parker 1922 v. 2 'To flow upwards, as water in a spring'
exclusion_reasons: base stone piʻi#0 carries a vulgar sexual sense in Wiktionary ('to mount, to breed' and an obscene synonym), in the same homograph as 'climb, ascend' (DECISIONS A4); Andrews piipii v. 3 'to vomit' (A11 treats vomiting as excretory; Andrews-only, so a P&E gate)
verdict_reason: A true repeat: Wiktionary gives the effervescing sense as 'Reduplication of piʻi (to ascend)', and Andrews brackets the verb [Pii, to go up], with 'to ascend; to flow upwards, as water in a spring'. It is held for the same reason as alapiʻi: under A4, P&E must show whether piʻi carries Wiktionary's vulgar sense (P&E via POLLEX gives only 'climb, ascend'). If P&E clears piʻi and has no vomiting sense under piʻipiʻi, it becomes keep.

gloss_source: Wiktionary poepoe verb 'round, rounded', noun 'sphere, globe'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'Round … globular'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of poe (round)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. poe#0 is 'round, rounded' (< PPN *poe 'pearl'; P&E via POLLEX poe 'Round (spherical)'), and Andrews has Poe adj. 'Round; circular. Syn: Poepoe'. Hawaiian Wikipedia uses poepoe for the globe and the hemispheres (poepoe hapa ʻākau).

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) pokipoki 'Sow bug, Pill bug (Isopoda)'; Andrews–Parker 1922 n. 2 'Sow bugs'
verdict_reason: Andrews pairs poki 'to stand or sit close together' with pokipoki 'to stand thickly together … to be multitudinous', and poki n. 'the cut worm' with pokipoki 'sow bugs'. POLLEX files P&E's pokipoki under PEP *poti 'bug species', with doubled cognates (Māori poti/poti, Tahitian po/poti). poki has no Wiktionary entry or POLLEX row, so there is no stone id (proposed 'poki'). The P&E sense names one small creature after another, which keeps the base only partly; the crowding sense is transparent but Andrews-only. P&E must confirm poki and which sense leads.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ponopono verb 'neat, tidy, arranged, in order'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of pono (correct)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. Andrews brackets it twice, [Pono, that which is right] and [Pono, rightness]. pono has one homograph (< PPN *pono; P&E via POLLEX 'correct procedure, correctness'), so the sense id is clear. 'In order, tidy' is rightness made visible.

gloss: tail feathers of a bird; streamer
gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) puapua 'Tail feathers of a cock; streamer'; Andrews–Parker 1922 n. 1–2
exclusion_reasons: P&E via POLLEX gives puapua 'rump, as of a chicken' under PPN *pua-pua 'genital area', whose only cognate (Māori puapua) is genital; DECISIONS A17 excludes kole on the same ground
verdict_reason: Excluded under §4.3 by the rule A17 applies to kole: a P&E sense sits on a genital etymon. It is also not a doubling of this PUA stone. POLLEX derives both P&E senses from inherited doubled forms (PPN *pua-pua 'genital area'; PCE *pua-pua 'spray'). Andrews' 'bundle of brushwood' [Pua, bundle] doubles pua 'a collection bound together', a homograph the stone does not include.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) pulapula 'Seedlings, sprouts, cuttings; descendant, offspring'
verdict_reason: Not pula doubled. POLLEX derives pulapula from PPN *pulapula 'propagation material for root crops' (Samoan pulapula, Tongan pulopula, Māori purapura) and PEP *purapura 'descendant'. Hawaiian pula is 'kindle' (*pula 'glow'), 'something in the eye' (*pula 'foreign body in eye') or a fish; none is seed or offspring. pula has no Wiktionary entry, so there is no stone either.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) pulepule 'Spotted'; Andrews–Parker 1922 'Spotted; speckled; of different colors'
verdict_reason: POLLEX files P&E's pulepule under PPN *pule-pule 'spotted', the doubled form, with doubled cognates across Polynesia (Samoan pulepule; Māori and Tahitian purepure). The base pule#1 is 'speckled' in Wiktionary, from PPN *pule 'cowrie', so the doubled word keeps the base's sense exactly. pule#1 rests on Wiktionary alone; POLLEX has no row for the free word.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) pulupulu 'Cotton'; Andrews–Parker 1922 n. 1–2 'Cotton … Tinder'
exclusion_reasons: sexual: P&E via POLLEX gives pulupulu a rare sense of sexual intercourse (under PNP *pulu 'hold')
verdict_reason: The cotton sense is plausibly pulu#0 doubled: pulu is 'fibre; boll of cotton', and POLLEX files P&E's pulupulu 'cotton' under PPN *pulu 'coconut husk fibre'. But P&E also gives pulupulu a rare sexual sense, and §4.3 drops the whole word when any sense is sexual.

gloss_source: Wiktionary punipuni verb 'to lie (tell falsehoods)'; Andrews–Parker 1922 n. 'A falsehood; a lie; a deceit'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of puni (deceived)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and the 'deceived' entry lists punipuni as derived. Andrews agrees: puni v. 2–3 'to deceive; to be deceived'; punipuni 'to be deceived; to be a deceiver'. The doubled word keeps the base's sense as an intensive. The sense id is right for 'deceived'; the stone needs the split in the note.

gloss_source: Wiktionary puʻupuʻu verb 'lumpy; heaped up; swollen up'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of puʻu (protuberance)', in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. puʻu has one homograph (< PPN *puku; P&E via POLLEX 'protuberance, lump, swelling', 'hill'), so the sense id is clear, and the doubled word is its plain plural or intensive.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pēpē noun 'baby (very young child)', borrowed from English
exclusion_reasons: loan: the attested sense is borrowed from English 'baby' (Wiktionary)
verdict_reason: pēpē is English 'baby', not pē doubled. Andrews does pair pe 'broken or flattened down; crushed' with pepe 'crushed fine; flattened', but Andrews writes no long vowels, so that word's vowel length is unknown, and pē has no Wiktionary entry or POLLEX row to make a stone. If P&E has a native pepe or pēpē 'crushed, flattened' beside pē, it can be put forward separately.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) pīpī 'Female ʻōʻō bird' (row flagged problematic); Andrews–Parker 1922 Pipi n. 'The female of the bird oo'
verdict_reason: Not pī doubled. The only stone pī is 'stingy; stinginess' (and the letter name P). POLLEX files P&E's pīpī 'female ʻōʻō' under PCE *pii 'young, immature' (Māori pii(pii) 'young of birds, chick') and flags the row as problematic. Andrews' pi v. 'to sprinkle … Syn: Pipi' may point to a pīpī 'sprinkle', but Andrews writes no long vowels and nothing in hand gives its spelling.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pōpō noun 'ball, wad; loaf (of bread); bunch, cluster'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Ball, round mass, wad'
verdict_reason: Not pō 'night' doubled. Wiktionary derives pōpō from PPN *popo < PCP *poo-poo, 'likely a reduplication of an extension of' Proto-Oceanic *posi; POLLEX gives PNP *poo-poo 'make into a ball by kneading'. The only stone pō is 'night; 24-hour day' (< PPN *poo 'night'), which the word does not keep. A PŌ·PŌ split would draw false lines to every night word.

gloss_source: Wiktionary pūpū noun 'shell (marine or land), beads'; POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert 1986) 'Shell, snail'
verdict_reason: Wiktionary gives the shell entry as 'Reduplication of pū from PPN *puu (conch)', and pū#1 is 'conch shell; any wind instrument' (P&E via POLLEX pū 'trumpet' < PPN *puu 'trumpet shell'). POLLEX's P&E pūpū 'shell, snail' < PPN *puupuu 'univalve shellfish' agrees. Shells in general, named from the conch, is a plain plural or likeness.

gloss_source: Wiktionary tūtū noun 'grandma, grandpa'
verdict_reason: No source gives a base tū: there is no Wiktionary entry, POLLEX row or Andrews entry for it, and Wiktionary gives tūtū no etymology. There is no stone to double.

gloss_source: Wiktionary uaua ("tough, sinewy, glutinous, viscid, leathery"); POLLEX (P&E) uaua "sinewy, tough, glutinous, viscid"
exclusion_reasons: slur: Andrews–Parker's second Uaua entry is 'a vulgar and derisive expression of contempt' for a person ruined by dissipation
verdict_reason: Not rain doubled. Wiktionary derives uaua from PPN *uaua 'tendon, vein', a reduplication of PPN *ua 'sinew' made 'likely to avoid conflation with ua (rain)'; POLLEX files P&E uaua under *ua 'vein, artery, tendon, sinew'. Hawaiian has no base ua 'sinew' in these sources, so UA·UA would show 'rain' twice. Andrews also carries a derisive, vulgar sense (§4.3).

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Uhiuhi v. 1 ("to cover in a temporary manner; to thatch or cover as a makeshift")
verdict_reason: Andrews' verb uhiuhi 'to cover temporarily, thatch as a makeshift' is plainly uhi#1 'to cover' doubled (no bracket, but the sense is the base's). The spelling uhiuhi is a P&E headword (POLLEX) and uhi takes no ʻokina or kahakō, but that headword is the tree. P&E must show a verb uhiuhi 'to cover'. If P&E has only the tree and the herb, drop.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) uhāuhā "pant, puff, as a dog, or as the wind"
exclusion_reasons: sexual: Andrews–Parker Uhauha v. 2 'to live in every indulgence of passion' (licentious); excretory/bodily discharge on the base: Andrews–Parker Uha v. 'to belch; to hawk up mucus' (compare DECISIONS A11)
verdict_reason: There is no UHĀ stone to double. Andrews' uhauha 'wasteful, prodigal' sits beside Andrews' uha 'wasteful', and P&E's uhāuhā 'pant, puff' (via POLLEX) suggests a base 'pant', so a reduplication is likely. But the word carries a licentious sense, and the base a belching/mucus sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ukiuki ("annoyed, displeased, vexed"; "anger; resentment")
verdict_reason: The living word ukiuki 'annoyed, anger' (Wiktionary; Hawaiian Wikipedia 'ka ukiuki a me ka kaumaha') is not traced to uki: Wiktionary suggests PPN *quti 'bite'. Only Andrews' older ukiuki 'offensive odour' echoes his uki 'to smell unpleasantly'. Even that has no stone to double.

gloss_source: Wiktionary uliuli ("blue, green, black, any dark color"); Andrews–Parker Uliuli adj. ("blue; green; dark colored; black: ka moana uliuli")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of uli' (Hawaiian reduplications), with the base sense kept: dark colour → any dark colour, deep blue. Andrews agrees. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword, and Hawaiian Wikipedia uses uliuli for blue in flag descriptions. No §4.3 sense on the word or on uli#0. P&E check is routine.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) umauma "chest, breast"; Andrews–Parker Umauma n. ("the breast; the bosom; the chest")
verdict_reason: POLLEX files P&E umauma 'chest' under PPN *uma 'chest, upper body'. It files P&E uma 'hand-wrestling' under a separate PCE *uma. In these sources Hawaiian keeps 'chest' only in the doubled form, so UMA·UMA would show 'hand-wrestling' twice. The doubled word does not keep the base's sense.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) unauna "hermit crabs in general"
verdict_reason: Andrews brackets Unauna 'tired, exhausted' as [Una, weary], so that sense is a reduplication. But una 'weary' is not among the base stones, and the living P&E headword unauna is the hermit crab, from a different etymon. On the only stone, UNA·UNA would read 'turtle shell' twice and mean neither.

gloss_source: Wiktionary waiwai ("to be rich"); POLLEX (P&E) waiwai "goods, property...wealth...rich"; Andrews–Parker Waiwai n. ("goods; property")
verdict_reason: This is a reduplication: Wiktionary category 'Hawaiian reduplications' says it is 'more likely, a reduplication of wai, a rare form of waiho (to leave, deposit)'. POLLEX files P&E waiwai with P&E wai 'to retain, place, leave, remain, earn, deposit' under PPN *qai. What is retained or earned becomes goods and wealth, so the sense is kept only partly: a reader will not see 'rich' in 'deposit' without the card's help. The spelling is attested twice. Pending: P&E should confirm that waiwai derives from wai 'deposit' rather than 'water' (Wiktionary allows both), and the designer should accept a WAI#1 stone.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) wanawana "spiny, thorny"; Andrews–Parker Wanawana adj. ("having sharp points; thorny; spiny")
verdict_reason: POLLEX reconstructs the word as the reduplication PPN *wana-wana 'spiny, prickly', and Andrews defines wanawana as 'covered with sharp points like the wana (sea-urchin)'. The doubled word keeps the base by likeness: spiny like the long-spined urchin. The spelling is a P&E headword (POLLEX). No §4.3 sense on the word or the base. Wiktionary has no wanawana entry, so P&E is the only printed source.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) waʻawaʻa "hollow at meeting of bones below the Adam's apple"
verdict_reason: Not canoe doubled. POLLEX files P&E waʻawaʻa under its own etymon, PPN *waka-waka 'thorax, rib-cage'. Andrews' senses (plump; ignorant; the upper thorax; a lobster's leg) do not build on waʻa 'canoe' either. WAʻA·WAʻA would be a false analysis.

gloss_source: Wiktionary wehewehe ("to explain"; "to open something up or pull two things apart"); Andrews–Parker Wehewehe v. [Wehe, to open] ("to open frequently; to open, that is, to expound")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of wehe'. Andrews brackets it [Wehe, to open] and glosses 'to open frequently; to open, that is, to expound'. Frequentative opening → explaining keeps the base sense, and Wiktionary keeps the literal 'open up, pull apart' too. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. Base wehe is P&E 'open, undo, untie, loosen' (POLLEX). No §4.3 sense on the word or the base.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Welawela adj. [Wela, hot] ("very hot"; "parched; dried up; scorched")
exclusion_reasons: base sense: Wiktionary wela (noun) lists 'lust, passion' beside 'heat; fever'. Under DECISIONS A1 this is a root-level question for the kumu, not a sense of welawela itself
verdict_reason: This is an intensive reduplication: Andrews brackets [Wela, hot] and glosses 'very hot'. But (1) the only source for the word is Andrews: there is no Wiktionary headword, and the POLLEX row in the dossier is for wela, not welawela. The spelling is pieced from Andrews plus the diacritic-free base wela (Wiktionary, POLLEX). (2) Wiktionary gives the base WELA a 'lust, passion' sense, which §4.3 read strictly would exclude. If the kumu clears WELA under A1 option 3 and P&E prints welawela, it becomes keep-pending.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) welewele "suspended, hanging"
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts P&E welewele 'suspended, hanging' and wele 'fine, thin (as thread)' in one set (PEP *were-were 'hanging membrane or flesh'), so the two are related. Which one is the base is not shown. There is no WELE stone, the senses only loosely match, and Andrews gives an unrelated 'to grudge'.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) weluwelu "shredded to bits"; Andrews–Parker Weluwelu adj. ("torn; broken up; ragged")
verdict_reason: A clear reduplication: Andrews brackets Weluwelu as [Welu, a rag], and POLLEX files P&E weluwelu 'shredded to bits' and P&E welu 'rag, ragged garment; ragged, frayed' in one set (PCE *weru). Ragged → torn to shreds keeps the base sense, and the spelling is a P&E headword. The sense is 'unresolved' only because welu has no Wiktionary entry and so no stone id. Pending: add a WELU stone (P&E 'rag; ragged, frayed', PCE *weru; DECISIONS B8 'add missing roots') and confirm in P&E.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) weuweu "fluffy; bushy or fuzzy (as a beard); herbage, grass, greenery"
exclusion_reasons: sexual: Andrews–Parker Weuweu n. 2 (figurative) 'licentious practices in the open or out of doors'
verdict_reason: Probably a reduplication: P&E weuweu 'fluffy, fuzzy' sits under PCE *weu 'fringe', and Andrews has weu 'covered with down'. But there is no WEU stone, and Andrews records a figurative sexual sense of weuweu, which §4.3 excludes.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Weawea adj. ("red; reddish; spotted with red")
exclusion_reasons: sexual: P&E (via POLLEX) weʻaweʻa 'to help, abet or tempt, especially in love affairs; … procurer'; Andrews–Parker Weawea n. 'a procurer … in licentious matters'
verdict_reason: Only Andrews' adjective 'reddish' builds on weʻa 'red dye'. P&E's weʻaweʻa is a different etymon (PCE *weke 'offender') with a procurer sense, so the word is excluded under §4.3, and the base has no stone.

gloss_source: Wiktionary wikiwiki ("to be quick, to be speedy"); Andrews–Parker Wikiwiki v. [Wiki, quick] ("to hasten; to hurry")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of wiki' (Hawaiian reduplications). Andrews brackets it [Wiki, quick]. The intensive keeps the base sense: quick → very quick, hurry. Base wiki is P&E 'hurry, hasten, quick, fast, swift' (POLLEX, PCE *witi). The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Wiliwili v. ("to stir round … to turn round rapidly … to whirl")
verdict_reason: Andrews' verb wiliwili ('to stir round … turn round rapidly … whirl') is a plain frequentative of wili 'twist, turn, wind' (P&E via POLLEX), and Wiktionary lists wiliwili under Hawaiian reduplications. The spelling is attested (Wiktionary, POLLEX). Pending because the verb sense is Andrews-only in these sources, while P&E (via POLLEX) and Wiktionary both lead with the tree. P&E must show the verb 'to twist repeatedly, whirl'. If it gives only the tree, the word becomes doubtful.

gloss_source: Wiktionary wīwī ("thin, slender"); Andrews–Parker Wiwi v. [Wi, famine] ("to grow poor in flesh")
verdict_reason: Andrews brackets Wiwi as [Wi, famine] ('to be poor; to be shriveled up; to grow poor in flesh'), and Andrews' base wi is 'impoverished'. Wiktionary gives wīwī 'thin, slender' with no etymology. Lean from want builds plainly on famine, but only Andrews states the link, so it is likely, not shown. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. P&E should confirm wīwī as from wī 'famine'.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻahaʻaha (noun, "cordage"; "Reduplication of ʻaha (cord)")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻaha (cord)', glossed 'cordage' (Hawaiian reduplications). Cord → cordage is a plain collective. Base ʻaha#1 is P&E 'sennit' (POLLEX, PPN *kafa 'sennit, coconut husk fibre'). The spelling ʻahaʻaha is the Wiktionary headword and a P&E headword. No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻaha#1. P&E should confirm the cordage sense: POLLEX shows only the stance sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻakaʻaka (noun "laughter"; verb "to laugh"); Andrews–Parker Akaaka n. ("laughter; exhilaration of spirits"), v. ("to laugh") [See aka, to laugh]
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻaka' (Hawaiian reduplications). Andrews says the same, and notes under Aka 'to laugh' that 'the form akaaka is more generally used'. Laugh → laughter keeps the base sense. Base ʻaka is P&E 'laugh' (POLLEX, PPN *kata), and Wiktionary has one homograph, so the stone id is clear. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword and is used on Hawaiian Wikipedia. No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻaka.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻakiʻaki verb ("to snap constantly, repeatedly; to nibble (like a fish)")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻaki (to take a nip and let go)' (Hawaiian reduplications). The verb is a plain frequentative: nip → snap constantly, nibble. Base ʻaki#0 is P&E 'bite, nip' (POLLEX, PPN *kati). The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻaki#0. Routine P&E check.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻalaʻala "aerial tubers of bitter yam (D. bulbifera)"
exclusion_reasons: POLLEX files P&E ʻalaʻala under PPN *kala 'male genitalia' (flagged Uncertain Semantic Connection). This is an etymon-level sense, not a Hawaiian one; compare the kole ruling in DECISIONS A17
verdict_reason: Not fragrance doubled. The only base stone is ʻala 'fragrance, perfume' (Wiktionary, PPN *kakala). P&E's ʻalaʻala (via POLLEX) is a yam tuber filed under a different etymon, PPN *kala. Andrews' alaala is squid bait and scrofula. No source links the word to ʻala, and there is no Wiktionary entry for it. ʻALA·ʻALA would read 'fragrance' twice and mean none of these.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻaleʻale (noun "ripple"; verb "rippling, stirring"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻaleʻale "stirring, moving, undulating, tossing, rippling"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻale (billow)' (Hawaiian reduplications). POLLEX files P&E ʻaleʻale under PCE *kale-kale 'agitated (of sea or water surface)', and P&E ʻale 'wave, billow; to ripple, stir' under PNP *kale. Andrews gives aleale as 'syn.' of ale 'to stir up, as water'. Wave → rippling, stirring keeps the base sense. Spelling attested twice (Wiktionary headword, POLLEX). No §4.3 sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻaloʻalo ("frequentative of ʻalo (to dodge)"; "evasive"); Andrews–Parker Aloalo v. [Freq. of alo, to dodge] ("to dodge rapidly or continuously")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻalo (to dodge)', glossed 'frequentative of ʻalo' (Hawaiian reduplications). Andrews brackets it [Freq. of alo, to dodge]. Base ʻalo is P&E 'dodge, evade, elude, avoid' (POLLEX, PPN *kalo), one homograph. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻaluʻalu verb ("loose, flabby, slack; to sag; wrinkled, uneven, rough"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻaluʻalu "loose, flabby … slack, as a rope; wrinkled, uneven, rough, lined"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻalu' (Hawaiian reduplications). POLLEX files P&E ʻaluʻalu 'loose, flabby, slack, wrinkled' under PEP *kalu 'loose, slack, wrinkled'. The base ʻalu 'to slacken, relax; to sag' (Wiktionary, PEP *kalu) is the same root, so the intensive keeps the base sense. The spelling is attested twice (Wiktionary, POLLEX). No §4.3 sense, but see the E1 note.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻamaʻama ("flathead mullet (Mugil cephalus)"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻamaʻama "mullet"
verdict_reason: Not a doubled base. POLLEX files P&E ʻamaʻama 'mullet' under a whole reduplicated fish name, *kama-kama 'fish sp.'. Wiktionary gives no etymology. The sources have no ʻama stone at all (base_homographs is empty). The POLLEX bases are ʻama 'talkative' and ʻama 'light, bright', and neither is kept in 'mullet'. Andrews' amaama adj. 'same as ama' (talkative) is the only doubled sense, and it has no stone either.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻamiʻami "elastic, pendulous, springy"; Andrews–Parker Amiami adj. (same)
exclusion_reasons: base is grammatical: the only ʻami stone in the sources is Wiktionary's locative preposition (DECISIONS B1)
verdict_reason: Probably a reduplication: Andrews' amiami v. says 'See ami', and Andrews' ami is 'a hinge; a swinging, pendulous motion; to turn as upon hinges', which fits 'elastic, pendulous, springy'. But that ami is Andrews-only. The only ʻami stone (Wiktionary) is a locative preposition, which cannot be a stone. POLLEX files P&E ʻamiʻami under PPN *kami 'open and shut mouth, gills' and flags it Problematic. No Wiktionary entry for the word.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻanoʻano ("seed"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻanoʻano "seed, kernel, germ"
exclusion_reasons: sexual/genital: Andrews–Parker Anoano n. 2 'semen'. Andrews-only (P&E via POLLEX gives 'seed, kernel, germ'; Wiktionary 'seed'), so a P&E gate under DECISIONS A1, not an exclusion by itself
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻano' (Hawaiian reduplications). Both words go back to PPN *kano 'flesh; substance, essential part; seed, kernel' (POLLEX files them in one set). But in Hawaiian, ʻano means 'kind, nature, character' and ʻanoʻano means 'seed', so the base sense shows only through the ancestor. Māori kano 'sort, kind; seed' keeps both senses on one word. ʻANO·ʻANO would read 'kind' twice and mean 'seed'. Two things hold it: the designer must accept that link (DECISIONS B9), and P&E must not carry Andrews' 'semen' sense (A1). If both clear, it becomes keep-pending.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻanāʻanā ("black magic, sorcery"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻanāʻanā "black-magic, evil sorcery"
exclusion_reasons: sorcery/death-prayer: P&E (via POLLEX) 'black-magic, evil sorcery'; Andrews 'a prayer used to procure the death … of one' (§4.3)
verdict_reason: Excluded under §4.3 as sorcery and death-prayer, whatever its form. It is also not a Hawaiian base doubled: Wiktionary calls it a reduplicated form of PEP *kaŋa 'place a curse on someone', and the sources have no Hawaiian base ʻanā (base_homographs is empty).

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻaoʻao ("side, flank; page of a book; group, team, party"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻaoʻao "side, boundary"
verdict_reason: Not a doubled base. Wiktionary and POLLEX both derive ʻaoʻao whole from PPN *kao-kao 'rib, flank, side'. The sources have no Wiktionary ʻao stone (base_homographs is empty). The POLLEX bases are ʻao 'new shoot, sprout' and ʻao 'dried baked taro', and neither is kept in 'side, page'.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻapeʻape ("any Gunnera species"); Andrews–Parker Apeape n. ("a variety of the ape (Gunnera petaloidea), having very large leaves and growing at high elevations")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻape (giant taro, Alocasia macrorrhiza)' (Hawaiian reduplications). Andrews calls ʻapeʻape 'a variety of the ape' with very large leaves, 'also known as ape lau nui'. The doubled word names a plant like ʻape: a likeness reduplication. Base ʻape is P&E Alocasia macrorrhiza (POLLEX, PPN *kape), one homograph. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense. The P&E check should confirm the plant sense.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻapiʻapi "filled, as a basket; abundant, as a feast"
verdict_reason: Two different words. Andrews' apiapi, 'the breathing of air dissolved in water, as a fish does', plausibly doubles Andrews' api 'gills; to flap, palpitate'. P&E's ʻapiʻapi (via POLLEX), 'filled, as a basket; abundant', comes from PPN *kapi 'packed tight' and keeps no gills sense. The sources have no ʻapi stone (base_homographs is empty, no POLLEX base row) and no Wiktionary entry for the word.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻauʻau ("to swim; to bathe"); POLLEX (P&E) ʻauʻau "bathe"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary's first gloss, 'to swim', is the base's own sense (ʻau#1 'to swim'), and 'to bathe' extends it, so the sense is kept. But no source says 'reduplication of ʻau'. Wiktionary derives ʻauʻau from PPN *kau-kau, and POLLEX files P&E ʻauʻau 'bathe' under a separate set *kau-kau 'bathe', apart from *kau 'swim'. So the link is likely, not shown. Spelling attested (Wiktionary, POLLEX), in common use (hale ʻauʻau). P&E should show ʻauʻau as built on ʻau 'swim'.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻawaʻawa ("sourness, acidity; bitterness"); Andrews–Parker Awaawa adj. ("sour; bitter; sharp; pungent")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻawa … Doublet of ʻawa' (Hawaiian reduplications). Bitter → sour, bitter, sharp keeps the base sense. The base's bitter sense is P&E (POLLEX ʻawa 'sour, bitter', PNP *kawa). The spelling is the Wiktionary headword, and Hawaiian Wikipedia uses ʻawaʻawa for sour or bitter tastes. No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻawa.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻaʻa "fibre from coconut husk"; ʻaʻa "brave, dare, venture, challenge, defy"; Wiktionary ʻaʻa
verdict_reason: Not a doubled base. P&E's ʻaʻa words (via POLLEX) come from PPN *kaka 'coconut fibre', PMQ *kaka 'envelope, sheath' and PPN *ma-kaka 'stiff, obstinate' ('dare'), each a whole form. The sources have no ʻa base stone (base_homographs is empty). Andrews' a is a particle, a conjunction and 'jawbone', and none is kept.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻehaʻeha ("extreme pain, agony; many small pains"); Andrews–Parker Ehaeha n. ("sorrow or mental distress; affliction; pain; grief")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary: 'Reduplication of ʻeha (painful)' (Hawaiian reduplications). The intensive and plural keep the base sense: pain → extreme pain, many small pains. Andrews agrees (pain, grief). Base ʻeha 'pain, hurt, sore' is one Wiktionary homograph. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword and is used on Hawaiian Wikipedia. No §4.3 sense. Routine P&E check.

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻekeʻeke "fussy, over-exacting, cranky"
verdict_reason: POLLEX files P&E ʻekeʻeke 'fussy, over-exacting, cranky' in the same set as P&E ʻeke 'cringe, shrink from, flinch, wince' (PEP *qete 'disgusted by'). Andrews' ekeeke 'dissatisfaction … dislike; displeasure' fits too. So it is likely the cringe root doubled: being easily put off becomes fussiness. No source says 'reduplication', and Wiktionary has no entry for the word. The sense is kept only partly. The spelling is attested (POLLEX). Pending: P&E should confirm the link, and the stone needs the B8 split from 'bag'.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻeleʻele (noun "black (color)"; verb "black, dark"); Andrews–Parker Eleele adj. ("black or approaching black; dark: he po eleele, a dark night")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives ʻeleʻele from PEP *kelekele 'dark, black', the 'reduplicated form of *kele', and gives the base ʻele 'dark, black' from the same PEP *kele. Andrews' ele says 'See eleele'. The doubling keeps the base sense exactly. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword, common on Hawaiian Wikipedia (Kai ʻEleʻele, the Black Sea). No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻele, but never print Andrews' English (above).

gloss_source: POLLEX (P&E) ʻeuʻeu "exciting, rousing, alert, lively, animated"; Andrews–Parker Eueu v. ("to rouse; to wake up; to stir up")
verdict_reason: Andrews' eu 'to rise, as from sleep; to get up; to raise' carries into eueu 'to rouse, wake up, stir up', so the sense is kept. But there is no ʻeu stone (no Wiktionary entry for the base or the word). The base sense 'rise' is Andrews-only. POLLEX files P&E ʻeuʻeu under PEP *keu 'move', apart from P&E ʻeu 'mischievous' (PMQ *keu). A stone made from P&E's ʻeu would show 'rascal'. P&E must show an ʻeu 'rise, stir' before this can be keep-pending.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): ʻeʻe "Hard, stiff, dry"; Andrews–Parker Ee adj. 2 "Hard; stiff; dry"
verdict_reason: Not a doubled root. POLLEX files P&E ʻeʻe 'hard, stiff, dry' under PNP *keke 'stiff, hard, inflexible', which is one two-syllable root, not *ke doubled. No Hawaiian base ʻe with a related sense exists in the sources: the dossier has no Wiktionary homograph and no POLLEX row for ʻe. Andrews' E entries are particles or ʻē 'other'. Andrews' three Ee entries (kind; downy; tidal, hard) show no base either. There is no stone for an ʻE·ʻE word.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻieʻie ("Freycinetia arborea, woody climbers with aerial roots"); POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) "Plant sp. (Freycinetia arborea)"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives ʻieʻie from PNP *kiekie, 'reduplication of PPN *kie (Pandanus species)'. POLLEX files P&E ʻieʻie under PNP *kie-kie. So the doubling is old. In Hawaiian, Andrews has ie n. 2 'a tall woody climber (Freycinetia) … see ieie' and n. 3 'the material used in braiding': a base ʻie with the same plant sense. But ʻie has no Wiktionary entry and no POLLEX row. That means it has no stone id, and its ʻokina is inferred from the doubled form. Proposed stone: 'ʻie' (ʻieʻie vine; aerial roots used in wickerwork; PPN *kie). Pending: P&E must confirm ʻie as a free root and its spelling.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻihaʻiha "… tight, tense"; Andrews–Parker Ihaiha adj. ("stretched tight; tense; taut")
exclusion_reasons: excretory: Pukui & Elbert via POLLEX gives ʻihaʻiha first as 'feeling of needing to relieve oneself' (PMQ *kiha 'tight, tense (bodily sensation)')
verdict_reason: No Hawaiian base ʻiha appears in any source in hand: no Wiktionary entry, no POLLEX row, no Andrews entry. POLLEX files the word under Proto-Marquesic *kiha, so any doubling is older than Hawaiian and has no stone. Separately, P&E's first sense is excretory, and §4.3 drops the word on that alone.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Ikeike v. ("See ike") → Ike v. 1–2 ("To see; to perceive by the eye … to know"); Wiktionary ʻikeʻike (verb, no sense line) "Reduplication of ʻike ('to see')"
verdict_reason: A true repeat. Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻike (to see)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and Andrews has Ikeike v. 'See ike'. Neither source says what the doubling adds: Wiktionary's sense line is empty, and Andrews only cross-refers. A card gloss today would just repeat ʻike's, which comes close to §4.3's 'teaches nothing'. The word is not in Hawaiian Wikipedia. Pending: P&E must give ʻikeʻike's own sense before it ships.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻikuʻiku "Stench; foul-smelling"; Andrews–Parker Iku iku n. ("An offensive smell. Syn: Okaoka")
verdict_reason: Not a doubled root. POLLEX files P&E ʻikuʻiku 'stench' under PCE *keto 'rotten' (marked phonologically irregular), and that protoform is not doubled at all. The only Andrews base is Iku, an interjection ('All at once! All together!'), which is grammatical (§4.3) and unrelated. Neither Wiktionary nor POLLEX has a base ʻiku. Andrews prints the word as two parts ('iku iku'), but no base meaning supports that split.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻiliʻili "Gravel"; Andrews–Parker under Pohaku ("small stones rubbed or worn smooth in the water were called iliili")
verdict_reason: Looks doubled but is not ʻili 'skin' doubled. POLLEX gives gravel its own PPN etymon, *kili-kili 'gravel, usually coral rubble' (Māori kirikiri, Sāmoan ʻiliʻili, Tongan kilikili). That is separate from *kili 'skin', the etymon of P&E ʻili, which is the only ʻili stone. As ʻILI·ʻILI it would draw false links to ʻilikai, ʻililua and the other skin words. It can still be a one-stone word under DECISIONS B7 option 1(b).

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻimoʻimo "To twinkle"; Andrews–Parker Imo v. 3 ("To twinkle, as a star"), Imoimo v. ("See imo")
verdict_reason: POLLEX puts P&E ʻimo 'to wink' and ʻimoʻimo 'to twinkle' in one set (PCE *kimo 'wink'; Māori kimo, Tongan kimo), and Andrews cross-refers imoimo to imo, whose sense 3 is 'to twinkle, as a star'. Wink → twinkle is a plain frequentative. The spelling is P&E's. The sense is 'unresolved' only because ʻimo has no Wiktionary entry, so it has no stone id yet. Proposed stone: 'ʻimo' ('to wink', PCE *kimo). P&E already prints the base (via POLLEX), so this needs curating rather than a new check.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker Inaina n. 1 ("Anger; rage; wrath"); spelling of this sense unconfirmed
exclusion_reasons: bodily discharge: Pukui & Elbert via POLLEX glosses ʻinaʻina 'reddish discharge preceding labour in childbirth' (PCE *kina-kina 'amnion'), and Andrews has 'the reddish evacuation which precedes labor'. Treated as excretory under §4.3. Unlike the A16 menses sense, this sense is in Pukui & Elbert, so it is not merely a P&E gate.
verdict_reason: This is not ʻina 'small sea urchin' (PPN *kina) doubled. POLLEX gives ʻinaʻina its own etymon, PCE *kina-kina 'amnion' (Tahitian inaina 'the water of child birth'). None of Andrews' three senses (anger; the birth discharge; to shake, stir) builds on the sea urchin. P&E's sense is also a bodily discharge, so §4.3 drops the word whatever the base.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻinoʻino ("spoiled, contaminated, rotten; broken, damaged"); POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) "Spoiled, contaminated, broken, damaged …"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻino (bad, wicked)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and POLLEX files P&E ʻinoʻino (PNP *kino-kino) beside ʻino < PPN *kino 'bad'. Bad → spoiled, broken, damaged is the intensive of the base. The spelling is attested twice (Wiktionary headword; P&E via POLLEX). Neither the word nor the ʻino stone has a §4.3 sense.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻiwaʻiwa "Maidenhair ferns (Adiantum spp.)"; Andrews–Parker Iwa iwa n. ("a species of fern (Adiantum capillus-veneris) … the maidenhair")
verdict_reason: POLLEX files P&E ʻiwaʻiwa 'maidenhair ferns' under PCE *kiwa 'a fern (Asplenium)', the same set as P&E ʻiwa 'a fern (Asplenium horridum)'. So it is probably the fern ʻiwa doubled to name a fern like it. That makes the sense kept only partly: Adiantum is a different fern. Andrews attests the word as 'Iwa iwa', the maidenhair; the dossier missed it. But the only stone id, 'ʻiwa', is Wiktionary's merged entry, and it leads with the frigatebird. POLLEX gives the frigatebird a separate *kiwa set. As it stands, a card would print 'frigatebird' on both stones. Sense stays unresolved until DECISIONS B8 splits off a fern stone (ʻiwa 'Asplenium fern', PCE *kiwa). P&E should confirm the derivation.
