gloss_source: none: Wiktionary's only sense is genital and is not reproduced
exclusion_reasons: genital: Wiktionary's only sense of ʻiʻoʻiʻo is a genital part
verdict_reason: §4.3 drops a word when any sense is genital, and this word's only recorded sense is. It might be ʻiʻo 'flesh' doubled, but no source says so (Wiktionary gives no etymology; there is no POLLEX or Andrews entry), and the question doesn't matter here.

gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻoheʻohe "Tall native tree sp. (Tetraplasandra spp.) …"; Andrews–Parker Oheohe n. ("A tree reaching a height of 50 to 60 feet"); Wiktionary ʻoheʻohe (Polyscias kavaiensis, P. gymnocarpa)
verdict_reason: This is ʻohe doubled. Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻohe (Polyscias sandwicensis)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and POLLEX files P&E ʻoheʻohe under PPN *kofe, the etymon of ʻohe. Andrews' ohe n. 3 and n. 6 name the same trees (Tetraplasandra, Reynoldsia). But the word keeps ʻohe's tree sense, not the bamboo sense that leads the stone, so the sense is kept only partly. The botanical names differ across sources (Tetraplasandra, Polyscias, Reynoldsia), so P&E should fix the species and confirm the sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻoliʻoli ("delight, enjoyment"); Andrews–Parker Olioli n. ("Playfulness; happiness"), adv. ("Joyfully; cheerfully")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻoli' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, glossed 'delight, enjoyment'. The base ʻoli is P&E 'joy, happiness, pleasure' (POLLEX, PPN *koli 'rejoice, be happy'). Joy → delight keeps the sense. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword, and the word is in everyday use on Hawaiian Wikipedia. No §4.3 sense. POLLEX has no ʻoliʻoli row, so the P&E check is routine.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻoluʻolu ("to be pleasant, nice"; etymology ʻolu "to be pleasant, comfortable"); Andrews–Parker Olu adj. 1 ("Comfortable; easy; pleasant")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻolu (to be pleasant, comfortable)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications. Andrews' olu 'comfortable; easy; pleasant' agrees, so pleasant → pleasant, nice keeps the base. But ʻolu has no Wiktionary headword, so it has no stone id: proposed 'ʻolu'. P&E via POLLEX glosses ʻolu 'supple, flexible' under PNP *kolu 'curved, coiled' (Andrews has 'limber' too). P&E must say whether 'pleasant' and 'supple' are one root before the stone's ancestor is printed, and whether the base has the Andrews 'sensual' sense.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻonaʻona ("dizzy"); Andrews–Parker Onaona adj. 2 ("Faint; dizzy, from weakness or want of food"); base P&E ʻona "drunk, dizzy and unsteady" (POLLEX)
verdict_reason: This is ʻona doubled. Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻona (drunk)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, glossed 'dizzy', and P&E's own ʻona (POLLEX, PPN *kona) is 'drunk, dizzy and unsteady'. So the dizzy sense keeps the base, and the spelling is attested. It is held because Andrews also gives fragrance and beauty senses that do not build on ʻona. F1 says the living sense leads. P&E must say which sense leads before the word ships as ʻONA·ʻONA. If fragrance leads, drop it as a repeat.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻoniʻoni ("to go or move back and forth, to wiggle … to move constantly"); Andrews–Parker Onioni v. [Oni, to move] ("to move back and forth quickly")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary derives ʻoniʻoni from PNP *konikoni and adds that it is 'also reanalyzable as reduplication of ʻoni (to move)' (Category: Hawaiian reduplications). Andrews brackets Onioni [Oni, to move], and P&E via POLLEX has ʻoni 'to move, fidget, wriggle'. Move → move back and forth constantly is the frequentative. ʻoni has no Wiktionary headword, so it has no stone id yet: proposed 'ʻoni' ('to move', P&E via POLLEX). Pending on curating that stone.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻopiʻopi ("to fold; folding"); Andrews–Parker Opiopi v. 1 ("To fold up, as a garment or tapa")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻopi (to fold)' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, and Andrews brackets Opiopi [Opi, to fold]. The base ʻopi is P&E 'fold, crease' (POLLEX, PPN *kopi 'double together, fold'). Fold → fold up, as tapa, is the frequentative, and the spelling is the Wiktionary headword. No §4.3 sense. The P&E check is routine (POLLEX has no ʻopiʻopi row).

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻukiʻuki ("Dianella sandwicensis of flax lilies, native to Hawaii"); Andrews–Parker Uki n. 1 ("A small shrub (Dianella odorata)")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary's ʻukiʻuki is the Dianella lily but gives no etymology. Andrews' first uki sense is the same plant ('a small shrub (Dianella odorata)'), so this is probably the plant name doubled. But no source states the derivation. The base ʻuki has no Wiktionary or POLLEX entry, so its ʻokina is inferred from the doubled form, and Andrews' uki entry mixes several plants (a grass, a tree, a reed). Proposed stone: 'ʻuki' (Dianella). Pending: P&E must confirm ʻuki as the plant and its spelling.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻulaʻula ("red (color)"); Andrews–Parker Ulaula adj. ("Red; rosy; reddish")
verdict_reason: Wiktionary has 'Reduplication of ʻula' in Category: Hawaiian reduplications, glossed 'red (color)'. The base ʻula#0 is P&E ʻula 'red' (POLLEX, PPN *kula 'red'), and Andrews says ula 'red' is 'written also ulaula'. Red → red, reddish keeps the base sense. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword, and the colour is in common use on Hawaiian Wikipedia. No §4.3 sense on the word or on ʻula#0.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻumiʻumi ("beard, goatee; mane"); POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) "Beard, chin"
verdict_reason: Not this base doubled. Wiktionary derives ʻumiʻumi from PPN *kumikumi 'beard', a reduplication of PCP *kumi (< PMP *kumis 'beard'). POLLEX files it under PPN *kumi-kumi. Hawaiian has no free ʻumi 'beard': its stones are ʻumi#0 'ten' and ʻumi#1 'strangle', and the beard keeps neither. As ʻUMI·ʻUMI it would link falsely to the number words. The one sense that does double ʻumi#1 (Andrews' 'to kill by strangling') is grim-only.

gloss: draw in a line aboard ship
gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): ʻuʻu "Draw in (of ship's line)", under PEP *kuku "draw together"
exclusion_reasons: sexual sense: P&E (via POLLEX, PPN *kuku "strip off") glosses ʻuʻu "to strip, as leaves or maile bark; to unsheath, as a sword" and also gives a sexual sense (masturbation); Andrews–Parker gives the same sense as a noun and as verb sense 2. Under §4.3, any sexual sense removes the whole word
verdict_reason: Not a doubled root, and excluded. POLLEX files both P&E senses under *kuku: PEP "draw together" and PPN "strip off, as leaves, bark". That is a two-syllable root with cognates kuku in Māori, Rapa Nui and Marquesan, not a doubled *ku. No ʻu base exists in the sources: it has no Wiktionary homograph and no POLLEX row. Andrews' U ("meditate; weep; drip; draw out, as a pencil") cannot be told apart from ʻū. His U v. 2 and Uu v. 4 do share "draw out, as a pencil from its case", but that does not give a stone. Separately, P&E and Andrews both carry a sexual sense, which §4.3 excludes.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻāʻā: "alternative form of ʻā ('booby')"; Wiktionary ʻā: "booby (any one of several species indigenous to Hawaii)"
exclusion_reasons: a sense is an epithet for a person: Wiktionary ʻāʻā "idiot, stupid person" (§4.3 slur; DECISIONS E3 drops epithets for persons); its other main senses name a disability as a trait: "dumbness", "to stutter", "dumb, silent", "dwarf, small person", "demented" (Wiktionary). DECISIONS E1 rules out disparaging disability senses, and a reader who knows them would hear them on ʻĀ·ʻĀ
verdict_reason: Most of Wiktionary's seven ʻāʻā entries are separate words: dumb/stutter/idiot, dwarf, demented, and the male ʻōʻō bird. The bird is POLLEX PPN *kaakaa "parrot", a whole reduplicated protoform, not ʻā doubled. None builds on ʻā#0 "fire": the burning sense is ʻaʻā, which Wiktionary derives from PPN *kakaha. One entry keeps a base sense: "alternative form of ʻā (booby)". That is a variant spelling, not a word that builds on the base, and it sits in the merged id ʻā#1. Separately, ʻāʻā carries "idiot, stupid person", which §4.3 and E3 keep out.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻēʻē (verb): "peculiar; contrary, opposite", "Reduplication of ʻē ('different')"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary says "Reduplication of ʻē ('different'). Compare with Māori kēkē from kē", and lists ʻēʻē among the derived terms of ʻē. The doubling keeps the sense: different becomes peculiar, contrary. Andrews agrees: E adv. 4 "in a contrary manner; adversely", with "See ee". The base ʻē#1 "strange, different" is PPN *kehe in both Wiktionary and POLLEX (P&E), so the sources agree on the id. The spelling is the Wiktionary headword. Neither the word nor ʻē#1 has a §4.3 sense. Routine P&E check.

gloss: tight, stiff, hard to pull out
gloss_source: POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert): ʻīʻī "Tight, difficult to extract, as a plug, stiff", under PEP *kiki "stiff"
verdict_reason: Not ʻī doubled. POLLEX files P&E ʻīʻī "tight, difficult to extract, as a plug, stiff" under PEP *kiki "stiff" (Māori ma-kiki, Rapa Nui kiki). That is a two-syllable root, and POLLEX's gloss ends with the note "Borrowed". The base ʻī ("to say; saying; supreme one") is PEP *kii "say", a different etymon, and "tight" keeps nothing of it. Wiktionary has no ʻīʻī entry.

gloss_source: Wiktionary ʻōʻō: "spade; digging stick" (< PPN *koho); POLLEX (Pukui & Elbert) ʻōʻō "Digging-stick"
verdict_reason: Wiktionary lists ʻōʻō among the derived terms of ʻō "to pierce", and gives both words the same etymon, PPN *koho "digging stick, husking stake". It calls them doublets. POLLEX (P&E) files both ʻō "sharp-pointed stick, coconut husker" and ʻōʻō "digging-stick" under *koho. So ʻōʻō is ʻō doubled, and it keeps the sense: a pointed stick for piercing becomes the pointed stick that breaks the ground. Tahitian ʻō covers both the husking stake and the digging stick. Andrews describes the ʻōʻō as hard wood "flattened and sharpened at one end for digging". The spelling is the Wiktionary headword and the POLLEX form. Neither the word nor ʻō#0 has a §4.3 sense. Routine P&E check of the entry.

gloss_source: Andrews–Parker 1922 Uu (u-u') n. 2: "A groan; a moaning; a low murmuring sound" (Andrews only; not yet a P&E gloss)
verdict_reason: The repeat rests on Andrews alone. His Uu (u-u') entry gives "a groan; a moaning; a low murmuring sound" beside "a stammering" and the squirrelfish. P&E (via POLLEX) spell those two ʻūʻū, so the groan sense is probably ʻūʻū as well, and it would be the frequentative of Wiktionary's ʻū "to groan, sigh". But the senses P&E attests through POLLEX are squirrelfish (PCE *kuu) and stutter (PPN *kuhu). Neither is shown to build on ʻū "grief; groan", and ʻū has no etymon in the sources. Before it could be kept, P&E must show ʻūʻū "groan, moan", and a kumu must rule on the ʻuʻu near-homograph.
